newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil may soon be more cocoa consumer than grower.
newsitem.headline: Brazil may soon be more cocoa consumer than grower.

text.p: Brazil, formerly the world's second largest cocoa producer, may in future be known more as a consumer given declining production due to disease and a growing domestic chocolate market, processing officials said.

"Brazil will have to be seen as a strong consuming country but a consumer which also produces a signficant amount," said Wady Jasmin, president of Joanes Industrial, a subsidiary of the U.K's E.D. and F. Man.

According to the Man Cocoa report in May, Brazilian cocoa production, battling against witch's broom disease, will fall short of grindings in 1996/97 (October/September), reaching only 156,000 tonnes against grindings of 185,000 tonnes.
Processors are moreover anticipating continued growth in the local market following a surge in chocolate demand stemming from the success of an anti-inflation plan begun in July 1994.
"We expect the regional market to grow in coming years," said Dirk Visser, cocoa account manager for the Brazilian arm of the U.S.' Cargill Inc.
"Growth has been phenomenal since the "real" plan, about 10 percent a year, and we think it should continue at about seven percent a year in the next five to six years," he added.
In the 1996/97 Brazilian crop year (May/April), output in the key Bahia region reached 2.90 million bags (174,000 tonnes) against local grindings of 169,071 tonnes, officials said.

Total Brazilian grindings Visser estimates at around 180,000 tonnes annually, of which 120,000 tonnes are processed for the Brazilian market, 30,000 tonnes for Mercosul countries and 30,000 tonnes for other destinations.
With production forecasts for 1997/98 of between 2.3 million to 2.7 million bags (138,000 to 162,000 tonnes), processors have already accepted the only option they have is to import.
Already this crop year Indonesian cocoa has been brought in and industries have a lso asked the government to carry out a risk assessment study of African cocoa.
Views over the prospects for recovery for Brazilian cocoa production are mixed.
New strains of the cocoa plant have recently been discovered to be more productive and more resistant to witch's broom disease than existing strains.
But resources will need to be made available to debt-ridden farmers if they are to continue to invest in cocoa.

"The technological problem presented by witch's broom is almost resolved. Now the problem is economic. Cocoa is already very labor-intensive. With witch's broom, it is super labor-intensive," Jasmin said.
Jasmin believes realistic forecasts of Brazilian production over the next 10 years are between 100,000 to 150,000 tonnes.

But Cargill's Visser is more optimistic a recovery in world cocoa prices since February this year has already started to be reflected in better husbandry which should eventually lead to higher production.
"We can clearly see that people making efforts. I think the worst is ... over," Visser said.
Apart from the 180,000 tonnes of grinding capacity already in use, a further 80,000 tonnes is currently standing idle in Brazil but could be started up again, he added.
Cargill which is the largest processor in Brazil currently has an annual capacity of 60,000 tonnes which it plans to expand to 85,000 tonnes in the coming years, he said.
Joanes last month signed an agreement with U.S. agribusiness giant Archer Daniels Midland (ADM) to sell its processing activities which include 50,000 tonnes in Brazil.
"This is very positive for the region as ADM is a very strong group which will no doubt make further investments," Jasmin said.
((-- Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151))
